blocks.text: A well engineered prompt is rarely one undifferentiated block of text, it is usually built from a handful of distinct, recognizable parts, each doing a different job, this topic covers that overall anatomy before the rest of this module dedicates a full topic to each individual part.

This topic introduces the four core components, instruction, context, input, and output format, along with the optional fifth component, examples, giving you a map for the more detailed topics that follow immediately after this one.
1. A Prompt Has Recognizable Parts
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473063660-903293730.png

Even a short, casual looking prompt usually contains identifiable pieces, a task being requested, background information relevant to that task, the actual content to act on, and a hint about how the response should look, prompt engineering gets much easier once you can recognize these pieces separately.
2. The Four Core Components
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064313-732564767.png

Instruction is what task the model should perform, context is background information relevant to that task, input is the specific content the instruction should be applied to, and output format is a specification of how the response should be structured, each of these gets its own dedicated topic immediately following this one.
3. Blob Prompts vs Structured Prompts
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064314-217113426.png

Suppose you write "Summarize this: [long article text] make it short and formal", all four components are technically present, but blended together without clear separation, a structured version separates them explicitly, an instruction line, a formatting note, and the input clearly marked apart from the rest.

code.content:
# Blob style
"Summarize this: [article text] make it short and formal"

# Structured style
"""
Instruction: Summarize the following article.
Output format: 2-3 sentences, formal tone.

Article:
[article text]
"""

blocks.text: 4. Examples as an Optional Fifth Component

blocks.alt: Examples as an Optional Fifth Component
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064315-442709564.png

A fifth component, one or more examples showing the desired input and output pattern, is optional but often powerful, this technique, few-shot prompting, gets its own full treatment in the next module, Prompting Fundamentals.

blocks.text: 5. What Happens When a Component Is Missing

blocks.alt: What Happens When a Component Is Missing
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064315-232426582.png

Leaving out the instruction and only providing input text forces the model to guess what task you actually want performed, sometimes it guesses reasonably, sometimes it guesses wrong, an explicit instruction removes that guesswork entirely.

blocks.alt: What Happens When a Component Is Missing
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064316-441572456.png

blocks.title: Missing components are the most common source of inconsistency
blocks.content: Many prompt engineering problems that look mysterious at first turn out to be one of these four components missing or left implicit, checking for all four is often the fastest way to debug a misbehaving prompt.

blocks.text: 6. Why Separating These Components Helps

Clearly separating instruction, context, input, and output format, even with simple labels or delimiters, covered in depth in the later Delimiter-Based Prompting topic, makes it much easier for the model to correctly identify what each piece of text is actually for, reducing the chance it confuses input content for part of the instruction.
7. A Full Anatomy, Assembled

Putting all the pieces together, a well formed prompt states the instruction clearly, supplies only the context genuinely relevant to that instruction, marks the input distinctly, and specifies the output format explicitly, this is the structural skeleton the rest of this module builds detailed techniques on top of.
8. This Anatomy Scales From Simple to Complex Prompts

A short, casual prompt might handle all four components implicitly and still work fine for a simple task, a production prompt handling varied, high stakes inputs benefits from making every one of these components explicit, this anatomy applies at both ends of that spectrum, just with varying amounts of explicit structure.
9. What the Rest of This Module Covers

blocks.alt: What the Rest of This Module Covers
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473064317-235530551.png

The next four topics in this module, Instruction, Context, Input, and Output Format, each take one of these components and go into real depth on how to write it well, followed by System Prompts vs User Prompts and Prompt Lifecycle, closing out this foundational module.
Worked Example

A developer writes the prompt "Translate to French: Hello, how are you?" and gets a correct but minimal response. Wanting more control, they restructure it using the full anatomy: an explicit instruction to translate to French, a context note about the target audience being formal business correspondence, the input text clearly marked, and an output format specifying just the translation with no additional commentary.

The restructured prompt now reliably produces exactly the translation needed, with the correct formality level, and without the occasional extra commentary the original minimal prompt sometimes added, demonstrating how making all four components explicit improves consistency.
Common Mistakes

items: Blending instruction, context, and input together without any clear separation, making it harder for the model to distinguish them
Leaving output format entirely implicit and then being surprised by inconsistent response structure
Including context that is not actually relevant to the specific instruction, adding noise without adding value
Assuming every prompt needs all five components in full, when a simple task may only need instruction and input

blocks.text: Practice

Take a prompt you have written casually before, and rewrite it by explicitly labeling each of the four core components, instruction, context, input, and output format, then compare whether the restructured version produces a more consistent output.
Key Takeaway

A prompt is built from recognizable parts, instruction, context, input, and output format, plus an optional examples component, and explicitly separating these parts, rather than blending them into one undifferentiated block of text, is one of the most reliable ways to make a prompt behavior more consistent and predictable.
